<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - This is a standalone backend service written in Go (with helper scripts in Node/NPM for CLI packaging) that implements a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Slack.  
   - It exposes an MCP-compatible endpoint over STDIO or Server-Sent Events (SSE), translates MCP “tool” calls into Slack API calls, caches workspace metadata, and returns structured responses to any MCP client.  

2. File Structure Analysis  
   - Top-level:  
     • cmd/slack-mcp-server: the entry point (main.go).  
     • pkg/: the core libraries organized by concern—handler, transport, provider, limiter, text, server, version, test utilities.  
     • Dockerfile & docker-compose*.yml: containerization and orchestration for dev, test, production, and toolkit debugging.  
     • npm/: cross-platform CLI wrappers for distributing the Go binary via NPM.  
     • build/: prebuilt extension artifacts (DXT), CI/CD packaging.  
   - Patterns & Config:  
     • MVC-style separation: transport → server core → handler → provider → external Slack.  
     • Rate limiting (pkg/limiter) inserted before Slack calls.  
     • Caching layers on local filesystem for users / channels (configurable via ENV).  
     • CI pipelines (.github/workflows) for unit tests, integration tests, and container releases.  

3. README Insights  
   - Describes supported transports (Stdio, SSE), authentication modes (stealth vs OAuth), features (history fetch, search, posting, caching).  
   - Environment variables govern ports, host binding, TLS, proxy, caching paths, log levels, and feature toggles.  
   - Two special “slack://” directory endpoints for channels and users.  

4. System Design Diagram Guidance  
   a. Main Components  
     1. MCP Client(s): any tool speaking MCP (via STDIO or SSE)  
     2. Transport Layer:  
        • STDIO transport adapter  
        • SSE transport adapter  
     3. Server Core (pkg/server):  
        • Authentication (pkg/server/auth)  
        • Request dispatcher  
     4. Rate Limiter (pkg/limiter)  
     5. Handler Layer (pkg/handler): maps MCP tools to application logic  
     6. Text Processor (pkg/text): formatting, parsing  
     7. Provider Layer (pkg/provider/edge + api.go): Slack edge client  
     8. Cache Store (local JSON files): users cache, channels cache  
     9. External Service: Slack Web API  
    10. CLI / Packaging: Docker container, NPM published binaries  

   b. Relationships & Data Flow  
     • Arrows from MCP Client → Transport → Server Core → (Auth + Limiter) → Handler → Text Processor → Provider → Slack API.  
     • Slack API responses flow back through Provider → Handler → Server Core → Transport → MCP Client.  
     • Caching: read-before-API-call from local JSON caches, write-after-API-call to caches.  

   c. Architectural Patterns  
     • Layered architecture: separation of transport, business logic, and external integration.  
     • Adapter pattern for transports and provider.  
     • Optional feature toggles via ENV variables (Strategy/Feature Toggle).  
     • Rate-limiting middleware integrated as a cross-cutting concern.  

   d. Key Technologies  
     • Go modules (go.mod)  
     • Docker, docker-compose  
     • NPM + cross-platform binaries  
     • GitHub Actions for CI/CD  
     • SSE & STDIO protocols for real-time and CLI use  
     • Local JSON files for O(1) cache lookups  

5. Tailoring Diagram to This Project  
   - Emphasize “dual transport” capability: show both STDIO and SSE adapters feeding into the same server core.  
   - Highlight the “stealth vs OAuth” auth module branching inside pkg/server/auth.  
   - Show the two directory endpoints (slack://…/channels and slack://…/users) as virtual filesystem mounts served by the handler layer.  
   - Illustrate the NPM wrapper and Docker container as deployment artifacts, but keep focus on runtime data flow.  

6. Diagramming Elements to Include  
   - Clear labels: e.g., “Transport Adapter: SSE”, “Rate Limiter”.  
   - Directional arrows: annotate with request types (e.g., “MCP tool call”, “Slack API HTTP call”).  
   - Color-coding:  
     • Blue for internal application layers (transport, server, handler)  
     • Orange for integration/adapter layers (provider, text processor)  
     • Green for external systems (Slack API, file system caches)  
   - Shapes:  
     • Rectangles for services/components  
     • Cylinders for data stores (cache files)  
     • Clouds for external services  

7. Final Tips  
   - Be exhaustive but modular: each Go package in pkg/ corresponds to one or more boxes in the diagram.  
   - Call out feature-toggle ENV variables alongside relevant components (e.g., SLACK_MCP_PROXY near the provider adapter).  
   - Use swimlanes or layered stacks to group “transport → business logic → external integration.”  
   - Annotate caching behavior and any middleware flows (authentication, rate-limiting).  
   - Keep the diagram readable: collapse low-level Go files into their package names; expand only when detail is needed.  
   - Validate with a dry-run: trace a sample “conversations_history” call through the diagram to ensure all components are represented.  
</explanation>
